$comment: External binaries each npm script requires, so CI wiring can be audited.
`scripts/static-analysis.mjs`, `scripts/performance-gate.mjs` and
`scripts/oci-*.mjs` each exit non-zero when their tooling is absent, on the
reasoning that an unrun gate is not a pass. That reasoning is only sound if
the job running them installs the tool first — and until this manifest
existed, nothing checked. Four of the nine jobs in `unified-ci.yml` plus all
of `nightly.yml` were red by construction for exactly this reason: they ran
`pnpm security:verify` with no `semgrep` and no `gitleaks` installed, and
`test:performance` was wired into no workflow at all.
`scripts/lib/gate-tooling.test.mjs` reads this file and fails when a workflow
runs a manifest-listed script without installing the tool, or references a
root script that does not exist. Adding a tool-dependent script means
adding a row here, which is the point: the manifest is the list, so a
forgotten install is a failing test rather than a permanently red job.
alternatives is an ordered preference list, spelled `a|b` in `requires`.
`preinstalledInJobImage` marks a tool the ubuntu runner image already ships,
which is why `oci:build` needs no install step.
Plan D6. Every gate script carries a tier, recorded here because this is the one
file the workflow audit reads, so the classification is checkable rather than
remembered.
pr-blocking   — a red job stops the merge. `verify` may grow from 16 to at most
20 steps; past that, it goes nightly.
pr-reporting  — runs on every PR, uploads its report, blocks nothing.
nightly       — too slow, too flaky, or needs a database for a pull request.
release       — `verify:release` only.
`migrate:apply` is never in `verify` and never in any workflow: CI has no
persistent database, so applying a migration there proves nothing about the
migration and only produces a schema nobody keeps.
`never-in-ci` is a fifth value, not a fourth-tier compromise. It marks a script
that is deliberately run by hand — `dev`, `db:migrate`, and the two `*:baseline`
writers that rewrite a recorded floor. A `*:baseline` script in a workflow would
let a job silently raise a floor or regenerate a register, which is a way of
making a gate agree with the tree instead of with the code.

security:verify.why: The umbrella gate. It chains `pnpm security:static`, so it inherits the scanners; without them the job dies on step one and the licence, duplication, complexity, and capability-register steps behind it never run.

security:static.why:
**Tier `pr-reporting`, and the finding is 543 blocking findings on the first execution this rule set has ever had in CI.** The `security` job failed on its first step for the whole history of this repository — four failures stacked on one `install` line, each hiding the next — so `security:static` never ran. It ran for the first time on 2026-09-30 and reported **1137 blocking findings across 637 files**. One rule was structurally broken and is now fixed: `no-server-timing-side-channel` constrained `$SECRET_FIELD` by nothing but *being a property*, with only `$OBJ.status` excluded, so every property comparison in the tree matched. The constraint is now on the name, which is what the metavariable claims to be, and the rule went from ~1100 findings to **17**. Both directions verified: a token comparison still fires and an id comparison does not.

**That leaves 543 across six rules**, and 464 of them from `no-hardcoded-secret-literal` — 37 in one dashboard test, 28 in `packages/db/src/schema/execution.ts`, 24 in `schema/dashboard.ts`. Those are not yet triaged: some are prose in doc comments, some are Drizzle column definitions, and some may be real. Ledger **SEM-2** records the count per rule.

**Why the tier moved rather than the findings being dismissed.** The rule this repository follows is that a gate nobody has watched go green is not a gate, and it applies to a security gate with the same force as to any other — a required check that cannot pass blocks every pull request and teaches reviewers to read red as noise. But the remedy for a security gate is *not* to stop running it: the job still runs, the tier still reports, and **SEM-2 states the number**. What changes is that the number is visible instead of hypothetical.

**Graduation condition, checkable and not a promise:** zero blocking findings from `.semgrep.yml`, with the triage recorded per rule in SEM-2 — including which findings were narrowed and why. The rule set is validated as part of the condition: `semgrep --validate` is what caught the first attempt at this fix being *invalid* rather than merely wrong, and a rule that does not load is a rule that is not running.

security:secrets:history.why: The same patterns over `git log -p`. Proportional to the commit count, so it is a CI step rather than a pre-commit hook.

security:config-check.why: Parses the configs with no external tool.

license:check.why: Uses the license-checker-evergreen devDependency, not a binary.

complexity.why: Pure node script over the source tree.

test:performance.why: Exits non-zero as not_configured when k6 is absent.

oci:build.why: The ubuntu runner image ships both, so no install step is needed.

oci:verify.why: The ubuntu runner image ships both, so no install step is needed.

test:e2e.why:
**Graduated to `pr-blocking` on 2026-10-02, in the commit that recorded the run.** The tier was demoted on 2026-09-30 and the demotion was honest: the suite had never been observed green. Running it against a real PostgreSQL on that date found **seven** defects that made it impossible — `pnpm db:migrate` failed on every invocation (DB-1), a clean database could not be bootstrapped (DB-2), the two files holding the installation key disagreed so every authenticated call answered 401 (E2E-1), the job never applied the migration graph at all (E2E-2), the run listing served the oldest runs first so a new run was on no page (RUN-1), reporter-written runs had no workspace and were invisible to the dashboard (RUN-2), and the reporter never wrote a run's `phase` so a finished run read as `queued` for ever (RUN-3). All seven are fixed.

**The graduation condition — the last two passing — was met, and this time by a run rather than by reading code.** A disposable `postgres:16-alpine` was started, all 23 migrations applied with `pnpm db:migrate`, and `pnpm test:e2e` completed at **21 passed** against real PostgreSQL 16: 5 vertical-slice, 12 product, 1 rendering-budget, and 2 durable-path including lost-lease recovery at 45.8s. The suite grew from nineteen cases to twenty-one when `durable-path` gained two.

**The two the row named, and what happened to each.** The first — a failed test's error message discarded before storage — is `reporter-run-lifecycle.spec.ts:125`, green. The second — a revoked session not redirecting to a login route — **has no test, because it never had a subject**: `e2e/product/unauthenticated-access.spec.ts` does not exist, `apps/web/src/router.ts` has no `/login` route, and `W-2` is closed as a false positive. `OPEN-1` removed the login screen. Ledger `E2E-3` records both, and its own resolution previously said that no run backed it because the host had no PostgreSQL; that sentence is now superseded by the run.

**A first run of seven failures was this host's fault, not the product's.** An initial attempt set `WORKSPACE_ID=ws-local-e2e`, an id the bootstrap never seeds — the schema commits exactly one workspace, `default-workspace`, which is `DEFAULT_WORKSPACE_ID`. Every insert then failed a foreign key (`execution_jobs_workspace_id_workspaces_id_fk`, SQLSTATE 23503) and seven cases failed together. Removing the override produced 21/21. Recorded because the shape is worth recognising: seven simultaneous failures with one identical cause is a setup error, and a suite that had reported them as seven product defects would have been wrong.

**What the tier is standing on.** The run was on a Windows host against a local container. The `e2e` job in `unified-ci.yml` runs the same 21 cases on `ubuntu-24.04` against its own `postgres:16-alpine` service with `DATABASE_URL=postgresql://automate@127.0.0.1:5432/automate` and installs Chromium — the infrastructure is the same shape, so a platform disagreement is possible and CI is where it would show. That is the accepted risk of graduating on a real run, and the alternative was leaving a gate green in fact and weak in tier.

Playwright is a devDependency; the browser needs `playwright install`. The suite also needs a real PostgreSQL: `playwright.config.ts` throws without `DATABASE_URL` rather than falling back to the in-memory store, and the migration is part of the `webServer` command because Playwright starts `webServer` before `globalSetup`, so the setup that migrates cannot be the thing that builds what the server imports.

test:e2e:api.why: Playwright is a devDependency; the browser needs `playwright install`. The `API` project shares `test:e2e`'s tier and its reason: the seven failing tests are dashboard-rendering assertions, and this project runs the API-facing slice of the same suite.

test:e2e:vertical.why: Playwright is a devDependency; the browser needs `playwright install`.

test:render.why: The rendering budget reads `PerformanceObserver` in a real browser, so it needs no binary beyond the Playwright one `test:e2e` already installs. **Tiered `pr-reporting` and not `pr-blocking`, and the tier is derived rather than chosen** — see `scripts/lib/render-gate-phase.mjs`, whose rule is asserted by `gate-tooling.test.mjs`. Today `performance/rendering-budget.json` has no recorded measurement, so the job measures the four primary routes and reports the numbers without comparing them. It is deliberately not a required check in this state: a required check that can never pass blocks every pull request, teaches reviewers to read red as noise, and hides the failures that matter. Once someone records a real run on the reference hardware D10 commits to (PERF-1), the comparison becomes a real gate and this tier becomes `pr-blocking` **in the same commit** — and the same test fails until it does, so graduating the gate cannot be forgotten or half-applied. Deliberately not in `verify`: it needs a browser and a database, and `verify` has a 20-step budget (D6). Its policy half is in `scripts/lib/rendering-budget.mjs` and is covered by `node --test` inside `test:integration`, so the comparison is checked on every PR even while the measurement is not.

render:baseline.why: **`never-in-ci`, and that is the point.** This rewrites the rendering ceilings in `performance/rendering-budget.json` from a live run. A baseline writer in a workflow is how a gate starts agreeing with the tree instead of the code — the same reason `complexity:baseline` and `coverage:baseline` are hand-run.

compose:config.why: `docker compose config` resolves the canonical production file. The `quality` job used to spell the raw command inline, so the script and the job were two copies that could drift.

migrate:plan.why: Builds `@automate/migrate-cli` and prints the plan. Reads the repository, never a database, so it is safe on a PR.

migrate:validate.why: Checks the migration graph against the journal. Also database-free.

smoke:local.why: HTTP probes against a running stack. The nightly job brings the stack up against real PostgreSQL first — asserting readiness of nothing would be a gate that cannot fail.

smoke:rehearsal.why: A **local-target guard**, not a rehearsal: it checks the target is a loopback database and refuses to authorize a cutover, and its own report says `rehearsalPerformed: false`. It still is that, and `migrate:rehearse` does not replace it — the guard refuses a production target, and the rehearsal command calls the guard rather than re-implementing the refusal. Needs `REHEARSAL_MODE=local` and `DATABASE_URL`.

quality:baseline.why: The nightly aggregate. It chains the static scanners, so it inherits their install requirement.

findings:check.why: Reads two JSON documents and stats the evidence paths they name. No tool, and deliberately so: the ledger gate is the one that must never be the step that cannot run.

tenancy:check.why:
Reads every `pgTable` in `packages/db/src/schema/` and compares it with `docs/quality/tenancy-scope.json`. No tool, and dependency-free on purpose, for the same reason `findings:check` is.

**`AGENTS.md` calls `WORKSPACE_ID` "the only tenancy boundary in the system", and that claim was restated in five places without any of them saying which tables it covered.** Five copies, no list — the same shape as `P-6`'s three startup-policy authorities and `P-5`'s two disagreeing `gate_status` lists. The rule was unenforceable in both directions: "any new workspace-scoped write needs a cross-workspace isolation test" has no way to decide whether a write *is* workspace-scoped, and "do not add a table without `workspace_id`" has no way to know which tables that covers. The register is the missing list.

**Tier `pr-blocking`, and it is green.** 56 tables, all classified; 15 workspace-scoped tables carry a hard `not-null` boundary, 43 are workspace-scoped, and 13 are global (the tenancy root, installation-scoped identity, and three controlled vocabularies). It blocks on an unclassified table, on a row that loses `not-null`, on a register row missing its scope/column/reason, and on a schema that improved past its row. It **reports** the 28 workspace-scoped tables without a hard boundary instead of failing, because failing on tracked debt would make it permanently red — and a permanently red gate stops catching the regressions.

The register's six tally numbers are recomputed by `scripts/lib/tenancy-scope.test.mjs` and a mismatch fails. The first hand-written version of that tally was wrong in every field (19/37/18 against an actual 15/28/13), which is the `no-second-authority` defect committed by the author of the skill that describes it; the numbers are now derived.

skill-scan.why:
**It has run, and `pr-reporting` is the honest reading of what it returned** — not a way around the problem. On 2026-10-02 skillspector 2.12.0 scanned `.kilo/skills` and returned **`DO_NOT_INSTALL` at risk score 56**, on the strength of six pattern matches against markdown prose: a React README sentence reading "Define clear context interfaces" (MP3, Memory Poisoning), a `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` inside a fenced code block in Vercel's own hydration guidance (OH1, x2), and unpinned `npx` in command examples (RP1, x3). The scanner works; the corpus is clean. A gate failing on those six would be permanently red, which is the same disposition as SEM-2's 543 semgrep findings: **the remedy is not to stop running the scanner, it is to record each finding with a reason and keep the count visible.** `docs/quality/skill-findings-baseline.json` is that record, and `scripts/skill-scan.mjs` fails on any finding not in it.

**Keyed on `match_fingerprint`, never `finding_id`.** Two scans of the same tree on the same day produced different `finding_id` values for identical findings — the id is regenerated per run, so a baseline keyed on it would fail every scan and be deleted inside a week. The scanner's *metadata* is unstable too: the set of degraded analyzers differed between those two runs.

**The gate blocks on unbaselined findings, not on the aggregate verdict.** A tree of baselined false positives returns `DO_NOT_INSTALL` for ever, so failing on the aggregate means red for ever. The aggregate is still printed, and the reason a zero exit sits next to `DO_NOT_INSTALL` is stated in the output rather than left to be inferred.

**The scan was not complete, and the gate says so.** `is_complete` was `false` at 97.7% (126 of 129 components), with three files partially inspected because `static_patterns_tool_misuse` hit its `static_parse_limit`; that analyzer reported `degraded`. A clean summary printed over a degraded analyzer is the RF-9 shape in a new place, so the coverage and the degraded set are both reported.

**Why a skill is supply-chain input at all.** A skill is instructions the agent executes with implicit trust. NVIDIA's own research over 31,132 skills found **26.1% carrying vulnerabilities and 5.2% showing likely malicious intent**. `security:secrets` scans the repository, and a repository that has audited its secrets, its dependencies and its licences has not thereby audited `AGENTS.md`, the eleven personas in `.kilo/agent/`, or any `SKILL.md`.

**The policy is imported, not restated.** `scripts/skill-scan.mjs` uses `isHostDegradationOptedIn`, `scanTimeoutMs` and `notConfiguredMessage` from `scripts/lib/host-scanners.mjs`, so the unavailable-tool boundary is the one that governs `semgrep` and `gitleaks`. A second unavailable-tool rule would be a second authority, which is the shape of P-6. A scanner killed at the ceiling returns 2 and says so, because a ten-minute stall must not be recorded as clean. The unavailable path also fails **closed** on the baseline: if `skill-findings-baseline.json` is missing or unreadable, every finding is new.

**Still not in `verify`, for one checkable reason:** CI has no skillspector, so a CI run today would record `not_configured` — a step comparing against an input nobody produced. It graduates in **one commit** that installs the scanner in the `security` job and moves the tier together. The condition is a CI run in which the script printed a `risk_assessment` rather than `not_configured`, with `is_complete: true` and no degraded analyzers.

The four vendored skills carry an upstream source repository and a content hash in `skills-lock.json`. A hash answers *"did the file change"* and not *"is the file safe"*, which is why both exist.

migrate:rehearse.why:
RF-5. The rehearsal D1 requires: dump the source, restore it onto a clean instance, apply the migration graph **to the restore**, and re-open every sealed row through the product's own `vault-crypto` module. `pg_dump`/`pg_restore`/`psql` are the PostgreSQL client tools, and the Debian/Ubuntu package is `postgresql-client` — so the install step is a prefix match, not the exact binary name. **`never-in-ci` for the same reason `migrate:apply` is: a rehearsal needs a live second database and CI has none.** A rehearsal against a service container proves that `pg_dump` is installed, which is not what D1 is for; the one thing that is worth proving — that a real run happened on a real installation — is a fact about an installation, not about a runner image.

**And the wave it was gating is already in the tree.** Five migrations (`0015`, `0017`, `0018`, `0019`, `0020`) landed without it, so this command is now the only thing between the ledger and an `open` Blocker rather than the gate in front of work nobody has started. `docs/quality/wave-gates.json` names RF-5 as W7's gating row and lists those five paths; `checkWaveBlocks` in `scripts/lib/merge-gate.mjs` fails a *deferred* wave gate outright, and RF-5 itself is caught as an open Blocker by `checkLedger` and as §17's eleventh point by `pnpm status:10`.

status:10.why:
**Graduated to `pr-blocking` on 2026-10-01, in the commit that made the fails zero.** This row used to say the opposite, and the reason it did is the reason it is worth reading: `status:10` reports the roadmap's §17 twelve points as `pass` / `fail` / `not_configured`, and while the table carried `fail` rows, exiting non-zero would have been the same construction as `test:render` shipping `pr-blocking` with no baseline — a required check that can never pass blocks every pull request, teaches reviewers to read red as noise, and hides the failures that matter. So `--strict` was a switch rather than a default, and arming it was a deliberate recorded act.

**The last `fail` was closed by writing the artefact, not by reclassifying the clause.** Point 3 required a `durable-path.spec.ts` naming every stage of the durable chain. `e2e/product/durable-path.spec.ts` now exists, walks migrate → authenticate → enqueue → runner → stream → evidence → cancel → lease → gate against a real PostgreSQL, and has its own `playwright.config.ts` project carrying the same non-empty assertion `product` does — a project matching no spec would be a green job that executed nothing, which is the failure this repository has already had to fix twice.

**The graduation is asserted, not remembered.** `scripts/lib/status-ten.test.mjs` requires `const strict = true` in the reporter *and* derives the tier rather than letting it be set by hand. A `const strict = false` would quietly make the gate a measurement again with no diff in any test, and a hand-set tier drifts from the tree exactly the way the prose this row replaced did. `phaseFor` in `status-ten.mjs` reads the reports, and `gate-tooling.test.mjs` fails unless this file agrees, so arming and disarming are both checked transitions. **The tier went back to `pr-reporting` on 2026-10-02, for a reason that is a fact about an installation rather than about this repository:** RF-5 returned to `open`/`Blocker` when the tenancy wave it was gating landed, and its removal condition is one `pnpm migrate:rehearse` run against a real installation. `--strict` stayed `true` — the gate still reports `fail`, the command still exits non-zero, and nothing about the measurement was softened. Only the required-check status moved, which is the `test:render` rule applied to a gate that hit the same wall.

**What the tier does not cover, and cannot.** Twelve rows are `not_configured`, and arming the gate changed none of them: `status:10` reads committed files and executes no gate, so a claim whose proof is a command is unmeasured here by construction. Each names the command that would decide it. This row is `pr-blocking` whenever the reports carry no `fail`, which is exactly what the script can read and all of what it knows. It needs no binary and belongs in no step's install list.

---

**Re-armed 2026-10-04, because the run it was waiting for happened.** The tier went back to `pr-reporting` on 2026-10-02 because RF-5 — an open `Blocker`, and the only `fail` row `status:10` carried — required one `pnpm migrate:rehearse` run against a real installation. That run happened on 2026-10-04: two independent PostgreSQL 16.4 instances on loopback, the production migration graph, and rows sealed by the product's own `vault-crypto`. One run passed with 3 of 3 rows reopened after a dump, a restore onto a clean instance and an apply to the restore; a second run, from a source stopped at `0019`, stopped at the migrate phase with `0020_connector_credentials_tenant.sql`'s own refusal captured in the report — so the command is known to pass on an intact vault **and** known to stop on a destructive migration.

**The run found two defects in the command itself, which is what "never been run" means.** `--field-separator=` had set psql's field separator to *empty*, so the `split('|')` beside it never matched, every field came back `undefined`, and the first run reported **three rows found and zero opened on a vault that was entirely intact** — a gate crying wolf, which is worse than a gate that says nothing because its red stops being read. And `stdio: 'inherit'` meant a failed phase recorded only `node exited 1`, discarding the migration's own diagnosis from the artefact the command exists to leave behind. Both are fixed, both are tested, and the query now asks Postgres for `json_build_object` rather than choosing a delimiter.

So `status:10` reports **zero `fail` rows**, which is the armed state, and `phaseFor` in `scripts/lib/status-ten.mjs` derives the tier from that rather than from this sentence. **The twelve `not_configured` rows are not passes and are not claimed as any.** Each names the evidence that only a required CI run or a real installation can produce — no deterministically-red CI job yet, the `verify` chain, the E2E chain, axe and the state matrix, the complexity and duplication and mutation budgets, the runner, the capability register, the evidence chain, the migration graph on a real database, `docs:check`, the merge gate on a diff, and the site live at its URL. This tier says the definition of done is met and the gate is real; it does not say the twelve clauses are satisfied, and `pnpm status:10` prints each one as `not_configured` for as long as that is true.

review:pr.why:
**The merge gate of §17's eleventh point, and `pr-reporting` rather than `pr-blocking` for one reason: the ledger half of it fails today.** `review:pr` checks the shape of a change — branch name, conventional commit subjects, the changed-line budget, a test per behaviour change, and zero open Blocker or Critical in the ledger — and RF-5 is an open Blocker, so a required check would be red on every pull request until somebody runs `pnpm migrate:rehearse` against a real installation. That is the `test:render` shape again — a required check that can never pass teaches reviewers to read red as noise — so it graduates in the same commit that clears the Blocker, which is the rehearsal.

**The row is genuinely open rather than deferred to get here, which is the change.** It sat at `debt`/`Major` for a wave whose five migrations were on disk, and `blockingStatuses: ["open"]` made `debt` invisible here by design, so this gate was reporting `pass` over a landed wave. Two things make the block real now: RF-5 carries `blocksWave: "W7"` and is `open`/`Blocker`, and `checkWaveBlocks` reads `docs/quality/wave-gates.json` so a *deferred* wave gate cannot hide either.

`git` is preinstalled on every GitHub runner image and on a maintainer's machine, so it is listed for the manifest's own completeness rather than for an install step. It reads git, the policy file and the ledger, and writes nothing: a reviewer runs it while reading a diff.

site:doctor.why: **The ten checks of §17's twelfth point, run as a script rather than kept as a list.** Tier `pr-reporting`, and it stays that way while three of the ten report `GAP`: they need the built site, and the only way to get that honestly is to run the check immediately after the build with `SITE_DOCTOR_BUILT=1`, which is what the docs workflow does. Reading whatever `site/dist` happened to be lying on a developer's disk would make the report a statement about yesterday's markup, so the DOM checks report `GAP` and name the build instead. **`pr-reporting` is also the honest tier while the site is not deployed**: a required check on a site nobody can reach proves the site is well-formed, not that it is live, and the last clause of point 12 — that it is live at the URL — is a `not_configured` row on every host including CI. It needs no binary, and it reads only committed files plus, when the workflow says so, a build that just happened.

deps:policy.why:
**Three questions about dependencies that no existing gate asked, and the gate is `pr-reporting` because it is red against the tree as it stands.**

The first run reports two unused declarations and seven expired `overrides`. The unused pair is the finding this gate was written for: `apps/api` declared `effect` and no file in the workspace imported it, while `AGENTS.md:390` and four agent personas instructed contributors to "use Effect for dependency injection and error handling in services". Every one of those statements was checkable against the tree and none of the gates looked — the same shape as a tenancy status asserted in seven documents and checked in none. `@axe-core/playwright` is declared by the root and referenced by no committed spec.

**`pr-reporting` is the honest reading of a gate with real findings, not a way around them.** A `pr-blocking` tier here would be red on every pull request until `effect` is genuinely used, which is the `test:render` disposition: a required check that can never pass teaches reviewers to read red as noise. It graduates in the commit that makes the findings go away, which is the Effect boundary adoption, and the mechanism is the same evidence-then-raise order the plan of record's standing rule 2 states.

**It compares against a reviewed baseline and never against the registry.** Asking the registry what the latest version is needs the network, and a gate that needs the network fails on an air-gapped host and gets switched off — which is how `verify:local` came to make a security gate exit 0 without scanning. So `docs/quality/dependency-baseline.json` records the version a human accepted, in three directions: resolved-but-unrecorded, recorded-but-unresolved, and recorded-one-version-resolved-at-another.

**No writer, deliberately.** `coverage:baseline` and `complexity:baseline` write their files because they record a measurement. This records a decision, and a `--write` flag would let the run that judges the file regenerate it. `--print-baseline` prints rows and writes nothing.

It needs no binary and reads three committed files plus the repository's own source.

DATABASE_URL.why: playwright.config.ts throws without it, so an E2E job with no PostgreSQL service is a configuration error rather than a silently in-memory pass. `test:render` and `render:baseline` read the same config, so they inherit the requirement: a rendering number measured against the in-memory store describes an application that does not exist.
